set.t: The Baptism of Christ (Dome Mosaic, Baptistery of Neon, Ravenna)
set.l: Baptistery of Neon (Orthodox Baptistery), Ravenna (in situ, centre of the dome)

summary: In the gold-ground medallion at the summit of the dome, John the Baptist stands on a rocky bank and baptizes Christ, who stands waist-deep in the Jordan while the dove of the Holy Spirit descends above him. At the right sits the personified river Jordan, a figure borrowed from classical river gods, as if witnessing the scene. Set directly above the font where Ravenna's Christians were baptized, the image showed every neophyte the event their own baptism repeated. It is one of the earliest monumental baptism scenes to survive in its original place.
facts: The octagonal baptistery was erected under Bishop Ursus around 400 and completed, with its mosaic decoration, under Bishop Neon later in the 5th century, which gives the building its name.

Christ's and the Baptist's faces, the dove and the jewelled cross are not original: Italian Wikipedia records that they were remade in a later (18th-century) restoration, so the central group is partly a modern reconstruction.
The medallion is surrounded by a procession of the twelve apostles, and the baptistery is one of the eight Early Christian monuments of Ravenna inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

set.t: The Baptism of Christ (Dome Mosaic, Arian Baptistery, Ravenna)
set.l: Arian Baptistery, Ravenna (in situ, centre of the dome)

summary: In the central roundel of the dome, a young, beardless Christ stands naked in the transparent waters of the Jordan while John the Baptist, in a leopard skin, lays his hand on his head and the dove of the Holy Spirit pours water from its beak. On the left the river Jordan sits as an old, white-haired god with a green mantle, leaning on an urn. Made for the Arian Christians of Theodoric's Ravenna and modelled on the older Baptistery of Neon nearby, it is one of the clearest early images of Christ's baptism, gentle and youthful against a field of gold.
facts: The baptistery was built for the Arian community under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great around 500, at the same time as Sant'Apollinare Nuovo; no documents record its construction.
Around the medallion the twelve apostles, led by Peter with the keys and Paul with a scroll, process towards an empty throne bearing a jewelled cross (the hetoimasia).

After Arianism was suppressed the building was reconsecrated for Catholic use, which is how its dome mosaic survived; it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Ravenna's Early Christian monuments.

set.t: Ivory Plaque with the Crucifixion and the Women at the Tomb (Liuthard Group)
set.c: Carolingian Francia (Liuthard group, probably Metz or the court school of Charles the Bald)
set.l: Munich (photographed in the Bayerisches Nationalmuseum, per the uploader)

summary: Within a deep acanthus frame, the crucified Christ hangs on a tall cross, his head turned and haloed, with the sun and moon in roundels above and a serpent coiled at the foot of the cross; soldiers offer the sponge and pierce his side. Below, the sea and the earth are personified, the earth as a woman with children, and further down the guards fall stunned while the angel, seated by a domed tomb, greets the three women. Typical of Carolingian ivories, the plaque turns the Passion into a cosmic drama in which all creation witnesses the death and resurrection of Christ.
facts: The Liuthard group of ivories is named after the Carolingian scribe Liuthard, who worked on manuscripts on which some of these carvings were mounted as book covers.

Carolingian Crucifixion ivories of this family characteristically add personifications of Sea (Oceanus) and Earth (Terra) to the Passion; the V&A notes that later Metz ivories borrowed this formula from Liuthard-group plaques.
Another Liuthard-group Crucifixion ivory forms the centre of the jewelled cover of the Pericopes of Henry II (Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 4452).
